items.title: Many languages, one common neural code
items.explainer: Researchers recorded brain activity of speakers of 21 languages listening to Alice in Wonderland, then used multilingual language models to build encoding models that predict that activity. A model trained on one language, such as French, could predict brain responses in another it never saw, such as Vietnamese. That suggests the brain represents meaning in a shared way across languages.
items.why: It gives language teachers new evidence that meaning, not surface form, is the common ground learners build on.

items.title: Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification
items.explainer: Teams of AI agents propose improvements to quantum algorithms, and a formal verifier mathematically checks each claim before it is accepted. The checker is what makes the agents' output trustworthy.
items.why: Pairing AI generation with an automatic checker is a pattern any teacher can copy for AI-assisted work.

items.title: GLM-5.4: a loop transformer for coding
items.explainer: Z.ai's new model is its first loop transformer, which runs some of its layers more than once instead of stacking more distinct layers. The idea is to get more reasoning per parameter.
items.why: Open models from new labs keep getting cheaper to run, which shapes what schools can afford.

tryThisWeek.title: Same meaning, two languages
tryThisWeek.steps: Give an AI chatbot one short paragraph in English and ask for it in a language your students speak, then ask it to explain three places where the two versions differ in form but keep the same meaning. Use the result as a five-minute warm-up on meaning over word-for-word translation.

hook: Could a model trained only on French brains read a Vietnamese speaker's brain?

lead.title: Twenty-one languages, one way of meaning
lead.dek: An MIT study used multilingual AI to show that brains across 21 languages seem to encode meaning the same way, which matters for anyone who teaches language.
paragraphs: The Fedorenko lab at MIT combined brain imaging from speakers of 21 languages with outputs from multilingual language models. Twelve languages came from existing data; nine more, including Korean, Mandarin, Hindi and Arabic, were recruited for this study. Everyone listened to Alice in Wonderland in their native language.

The team built encoding models that predict brain activity from the AI's internal representation of the text. They worked in every language, even ones with little data like Marathi and Lithuanian. The surprise: a model trained on one language predicted brain responses in a language it never saw, such as French to Vietnamese.

That transfer only works if brains share a common code, and the analysis points to meaning as that shared part. The work appears in Nature Neuroscience. It could also help clinical language tools reach speakers beyond English.
lead.against: Encoding models measure correlation with imaging signals, and a shared meaning component does not erase the real differences between languages that the authors themselves say must also be represented.
lead.watch: Whether the reverse direction, decoding language from brain activity, gets tried for endangered languages.
lead.ask: If meaning is the shared layer, how much class time should go to meaning-first tasks before form?

graph.title: How much training does a brain model need?
graph.tease: MIT researchers built models that predict brain activity from multilingual AI.
graph.question: To predict brain responses in Vietnamese, how many languages did one model need to be trained on?
graph.reveal: A model trained on French alone predicted Vietnamese brain responses. That only works if brains share a code for meaning across languages.
graph.caveat: One peer-reviewed study; counts are from the MIT News summary, and the French to Vietnamese case is the example the authors give.
